opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to the difference between losing because the problem was genuinely hard and losing because we just didn't do the obvious things.

There's a real chance that aligning very capable systems is fundamentally hard, that we hit some technical wall we don't know how to get past in time. If that happens, it's tragic, but at least you can say people tried their best against a difficult problem. What really gets to me is the other scenario: we actually had the tools, or could easily have built them, and we didn't use them. Maybe a lab skipped a dangerous-capability evaluation because it was racing a competitor. Maybe a model's weights got stolen because basic security hygiene wasn't followed. Maybe a safeguard was known to be trivially jailbreakable and it shipped anyway because nobody was accountable for fixing it.

A lot of my work at FAR.AI has been red-teaming systems, including showing that superhuman Go AIs can be beaten by fairly simple adversarial strategies, and finding ways around safety training in frontier models. What strikes me again and again is that many of these vulnerabilities aren't deep mysteries. They're things you'd find if you looked, and that you could mitigate with reasonable effort if anyone had an incentive to.

So unforced errors are painful because they're preventable. They don't take scientific breakthroughs; they take diligence, good institutions, and sometimes a willingness to slow down a bit. If we end up in a bad outcome because of those, it means we failed not on the hard part but on the parts that were within our reach. And I think that's actually a hopeful framing too: a meaningful share of the risk is addressable right now with things we already know how to do.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts genuinely hard alignment problems with preventable failures where available tools or safeguards were neglected, and says the latter are especially painful.

r002.rationale: It mentions racing competitors as one possible cause of neglect, but does not identify coordination difficulties as an understandable reason for failing to reduce an already small catastrophe risk further.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the thing that gets me is that there are some risks from AI that are genuinely hard. You could imagine a world where we've done everything right, we've put in all the research effort, we've been careful, and we still get surprised by something. That would be tragic, but in some sense it's forgivable. Nobody could have reasonably done better.

What I find much harder to stomach is when the failure comes from something we basically already knew how to avoid. The research existed, the warning signs were visible, and the safeguard just wasn't put in place because it was inconvenient, or someone was in a hurry, or the incentives pointed the other way. That's not a knowledge problem, it's a prioritization problem. And those are the cases where, when you look back, you can point to a specific decision and say, if that had gone differently, this wouldn't have happened.

A lot of what we see at FAR AI, when we red-team frontier models, falls into that category. We'll find a jailbreak or an adversarial attack, and it's not some exotic new technique. It's a variation on something that's been in the literature for years. Nobody tested for it, or they tested for it once and then shipped an update that silently broke the mitigation. There's no deep scientific mystery there. It's just that the evaluation didn't get done, or the fix didn't get prioritized.

And I think that's especially painful for two reasons. One is just the counterfactual. These are the failures we could most easily have prevented, so each one represents a missed opportunity. The other is what it signals. If we can't reliably get the easy stuff right, that doesn't give me a lot of confidence that we'll handle the hard stuff when it arrives. The hard problems are going to require real discipline and real investment, and the unforced errors suggest that discipline isn't there yet. So in a sense, I see them less as isolated incidents and more as a leading indicator for how we're going to do on the things that actually matter most.

r001.rationale: It contrasts unforeseeable failures after careful effort with failures where known research or safeguards were neglected, calling the latter more painful and preventable.

r002.rationale: It mentions inconvenience, haste, and misaligned incentives, but does not identify coordination difficulties as an understandable reason to leave an already small catastrophe risk unreduced.

astra-6.text: Because they’re so avoidable. There are genuinely hard problems in AI safety, and we’re going to have to work hard to solve those. But it’s particularly frustrating when a failure happens because we didn’t do a test we knew how to do, or we found a problem and didn’t act on it. In those cases, we didn’t need a scientific breakthrough—we needed to follow through on what we already knew. And with systems that are becoming more capable and more widely deployed, those seemingly mundane mistakes can have increasingly serious consequences.

r001.rationale: It contrasts genuinely hard safety problems with failures caused by not running a known test or acting on a discovered problem, calling those failures especially frustrating and avoidable.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention coordination difficulties or describe them as a reason for failing to reduce an already small risk of AI catastrophe.

sol-6.1.text: I think because they’re so preventable. There are genuinely hard problems in AI safety, where we don’t yet know what a good solution looks like. But if a system fails because we didn’t run a fairly straightforward test, or we knew about a vulnerability and deployed it anyway, that feels like a particularly unfortunate outcome. We could have caught it, and we could have done something about it. I’d like us to get the basics right so that we’re at least confronting the hard problems, rather than tripping over things we already know how to address.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts genuinely hard safety problems with failures caused by skipping a straightforward test or deploying despite a known vulnerability, and calls the latter particularly unfortunate because they could have been prevented.

r002.rationale: It does not mention coordination difficulties or reducing an already small risk of AI catastrophe.
